items.title: Buddy Collette interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999
items.q: And then what he’d finally do... So we all got ideas that it was a better sounding band with him playing cello. It really was because Jim Hall was there with the chords... We all felt the same way... we said well this band really sounds good this way.

ctx.x: And he brought his book, so then when I came to join them they were playing basically Bob’s arrangements. I brought a couple of charts of my own. And then Fred would actually play just cello solos on intermission. Because of that great energy he had. He wouldn’t take a break. Chico would say, “You want to do some cello playing?” He said yeah he’d do “Granada” and a lot of solos. But then what he’d finally do, he’d play too long and Chico was anxious to get back on the stand, especially if we had a packed house.…

items.title: Jim Hall — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Buddy Collette played the woodwinds... Carson Smith was the bass player, and Chico and me... The quintet. So it was a perfect job for me and we played at this club

ctx.x: I would really just like to know what your experience was with that. Did it click right away? Was it…? How, how did it [go?]?

Yeah, it was… Well, first of all, it literally was… I won’t say a lifesaver but I needed a job. (laughs) And I could, with my background I could, it would… Fred Katz played cello and piano. And then Buddy Collette played the woodwinds — clarinet and alto, and I don’t know if he played tenor. Carson Smith was the bass player, and Chico and me, I guess that’s it. The quintet. So it was a perfect job for me and we played at this club in Long Beach — The Strollers — for months. So I could write for the group and I…
We stick to the Chico group just for a minute.
